title: Uterine fibroid embolization
summary: Shrinks fibroids by blocking the blood vessels that feed them. No surgery.
lede: A way to shrink fibroids by cutting off their blood supply, through a tiny opening at the groin or wrist. No surgery and no general anaesthetic.
facts: at the groin or wrist, no stitches

chapters.title: Fibroids are growths in the wall of the uterus
body: Fibroids are made of muscle and fibrous tissue. They are not cancer, and they are very common: by age 50, most people with a uterus have had at least one.
Many cause no problems. Depending on where they grow, others can cause heavy periods, cramping, or pressure on the bladder and bowel. The model shows the four places they grow.

keys.name: On the outside

body: The model is built in separate pieces, like the printed one your doctor may hand you. Slide it apart and back together, tap any part on the model, or tap a name below to light it up.
It is cut open down the middle so you can see inside the uterus. The blood vessels are drawn larger than life so they are easy to follow.

chapters.title: Fibroids need a steady blood supply
body: Each fibroid is fed by small arteries branching into the uterus. Fibroids depend on this supply much more than the healthy muscle around them does.
UFE blocks those small arteries. Without blood, the fibroids soften and shrink over the following months, while the uterus itself recovers and stays in place.

chapters.title: A small opening at the groin or wrist
body: You stay awake, with medicine to keep you relaxed and comfortable. The skin is numbed, and the doctor places a thin tube into the artery there. There is no surgical cut.

chapters.title: A catheter travels to the uterus
body: A catheter about as thin as a strand of spaghetti is guided through the arteries to the ones feeding the uterus. The doctor watches it on an X-ray screen the whole way. Most people do not feel it moving inside the blood vessels.

chapters.title: Tiny particles block the fibroids' supply
body: Particles about the size of grains of sand are released through the catheter. They lodge in the small vessels feeding the fibroids. Both sides of the uterus are usually treated, through the same opening.

chapters.title: The catheter comes out
body: Pressure is held on the opening until it seals, and no stitches are needed. Time in the procedure room is often around 30 minutes, though the whole hospital visit takes most of the day.

chapters.title: Six months later, the fibroids are smaller
body: Without their blood supply, fibroids shrink over the months that follow, often shrinking to around half their volume. Heavy bleeding often improves from the first period after treatment.
The uterus stays in place. The model shows the idea. How much your own fibroids shrink depends on their size, type and position.

chapters.title: The orange markers show what can go wrong
body: The lettered markers match the orange discs on the printed model your doctor may show you. Tap a letter, here or on the model, to read about it.

risks.title: Pain, fever and nausea afterwards
risks.body: Common and expected. As the fibroids break down, most people have cramping, a low fever and tiredness for a few days. It is treated with medicine you take home.

risks.title: A fibroid passing out
risks.body: Occasionally a fibroid that bulges into the cavity loosens and passes through the vagina in the weeks afterwards. This can cause cramping or discharge.

risks.title: Periods stopping early
risks.body: Uncommon. If particles reach the ovaries' blood supply, periods can stop early. This happens mainly in people over 40.

risks.title: Bruising at the entry point
risks.body: A bruise or small swelling where the catheter went in is the most common minor problem. Serious bleeding is rare.

risks.title: Injury to an artery
risks.body: Uncommon. The team watches the whole route on the X-ray screen to avoid this.

recovery: Rest in recovery for several hours while the team manages cramping and nausea. Most people go home that evening, with a ride.
Cramping, low fever and tiredness are expected and usually peak here. Take the medicine you were sent home with.
Most people are back to normal activity in about a week. Ask when you can drive, work and exercise.
Heavy bleeding often improves from the first cycle after treatment and keeps improving.
Fibroids keep shrinking. Your team usually checks in with a follow-up visit or scan.
yourVisit.callIf: Call your care team if you have a fever that does not settle, pain that gets worse instead of better, foul-smelling discharge, or bleeding or swelling at the groin or wrist.
benefits: Your uterus stays in place. No hysterectomy.
No surgical cut, no stitches, and very little blood loss.
Recovery of about a week, compared with several weeks after a hysterectomy.
About 9 in 10 people find their symptoms improve a great deal or go away.
risks: Cramping, fever and nausea for a few days: common and expected.
Bruising or bleeding at the entry point.
A fibroid passing out through the vagina: occasional.
Periods stopping early: uncommon, mainly over 40.
Infection: rare, but can be serious.
Serious complications overall: fewer than 4 in 100 people.
yourVisit.fertility: Effects on pregnancy are not fully settled. UFE is not usually the first choice for someone trying to become pregnant, and Canadian guidance treats it as a case-by-case conversation. Raise your plans early so they are part of the decision.
alternatives: Many fibroids stay the same size or shrink after menopause. If symptoms are manageable, doing nothing for now is a real option.
Can reduce bleeding and pain, or shrink fibroids for a time, but symptoms often return when it stops.
Surgery that removes the fibroids and keeps the uterus.
Surgery that removes the uterus. It ends fibroid symptoms for good, with a longer recovery.

opts: By blocking the blood vessels that feed them
check.why: Tiny particles block the fibroids' blood supply, so they soften and shrink. Nothing is cut out.

check.q: Where does the catheter usually go in?
opts: At the groin, or sometimes the wrist
check.why: A small nick at the groin or wrist. The skin is numbed, and no stitches are needed.

check.q: What do most people feel in the first few days?
opts: Cramping, and sometimes a low fever and nausea
check.why: This is called post-embolization syndrome. It is common, expected, and treated with medicine you take home.

check.q: Is UFE right for everyone with fibroids?
opts: No. It depends on your fibroids, symptoms and plans, including pregnancy
check.why: There are other good options, including waiting, medication and surgery.
